paras: The ordering out of Black railroad laborers near Sheridan, Arkansas, took place in 1903, shortly before September 1, when white laborers ordered Black workers grading the Pine Bluff and Western railroad to leave. No violence was reported, and an officer of the railroad company said the trouble was over and had never been serious. The episode drew notice chiefly because the Sheridan Headlight, edited by a state senator, publicly called the order a mistake.

About seventy-five Black laborers were camped in De Kalb township, Grant county, doing grading work on the line, according to a correspondent of the Pine Bluff Daily Graphic. The same correspondent wrote that white residents nearby were not used to their presence and that it was "the first time they have tolerated the employment of negroes in that locality." The Headlight said the company had been willing to use white workers but could not get hands, hence its use of Black labor.

At an unstated date before September 1, white laborers ordered the Black laborers on the line to leave their work. The coverage does not say whether the Black workers left or stayed, and it names none of the men on either side.

The Headlight, whose editor was State Senator R. R. Adams, argued that the people wanted the road finished and warned that "such proceedings" were disagreeable to the authorities and could add expense for taxpayers. An officer of the company told the Graphic that "the trouble is all over, and never at any time amounted to anything serious." No report of arrests or of any official action appears in the coverage.

The only report found ran in the Pine Bluff Daily Graphic on September 1, 1903, under the headlines "ORDERED TO GO" and "WHITES ORDER NEGROES AT WORK ON P. B. AND W. TO LEAVE." The Graphic called it "some trouble with the negro laborers" and framed it through the Headlight's objection, which rested on the need for labor and the cost to the public. It closed with the company's assurance that the matter was minor, and no Black newspaper coverage of the episode was found.

accounts.label: Sheridan Headlight editorial
accounts.gist: The order was a mistake: the company had tried to hire white hands and could not, the road was wanted, and such proceedings were disagreeable to the authorities and could cost taxpayers.

accounts.gist: About seventy-five Black laborers were camped in De Kalb township doing grading; local whites were not used to their presence and had not before tolerated Black employment there.

accounts.label: Railroad company officer
